..
Issued at 1256 AM EDT Sun Sep 27 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Well defined nor'easter closing off the Mid Atlantic shore, which is 
retrograding a rex block ridge overhead. Ridge remains parked 
overhead into next week, as the blocking from the nor'easter eases 
once it gets set adrift to the east on the Atlantic into early next 
week. Meanwhile, stagnant northern stream flow will lead to the 
dissolution of a northern stream wave over the upper Midwest. 
Cursory glance at the 00z sounding this evening states that we may 
even struggle to get cloud cover to manifest until later today into 
tonight from this wave as it makes an attempt to intrude as it gets 
sheared out overhead. Otherwise, largely clear skies amid dry 
condition to prevail through Tuesday. 

Meanwhile, split flow prominently featuring an active subtropical 
jet reinforced by longwave troughing anchored off the California 
coast to unleash a torrent of eastern tropical Pacific waves into 
the central and southern Plains through the week, including the 
potential remnants of major Hurricane Polo currently churning off 
the coast of Mexico being ingested around / after midweek. Meager 
northern stream activity anticipated until a more potent shortwave 
zips through the upper Midwest and into the Great Lakes Tuesday 
night into Wednesday, but the lingering effects of rex blocking may 
shear this wave out as it approaches as well. Continued wave 
ejections coupled with a stationary front creating a barrier for 
moisture will stonewall deepest moisture pooling across the 
aforementioned region, potentially leaking as far north as the mid 
Mississippi and Ohio valleys later in the week, with increased, but 
still unimpressive, moisture streaming into the upper Midwest and 
Great Lakes through the remainder of the forecast period. With the 
breakdown in the rex block ridge and more zonal northern stream flow 
building, anticipation is that temperatures cool down to much more 
seasonable levels with low end shower chances into next weekend.

Details: 

Ongoing patchy fog will scour out through this morning. Otherwise, 
still quite quiet here in the Northwoods the next few days. 
Aforementioned decaying shortwave will lead to an increase in cloud 
cover later today into tonight, with the only major impacts likely 
being slightly warmer overnight temps (lows might only touch the 
30s, with 40s most elsewhere) and likely a reduced fog footprint 
across the region. As the pattern becomes regular again, return flow 
to build on the backside of the ridge as the trough axis folds 
eastward, resulting in warmer temperatures and sunnier skies Monday 
and Tuesday, with highs peaking in the mid to upper 70s across the 
board, and overnight lows in the 40s. 

As the aforementioned Pacific moisture plume intrudes Tuesday night 
into Wednesday, reinforcing northern stream wave to draw moisture 
into the region... but the wave will be on a downward trend, and 
current timing of this feature favors a nighttime passage. In 
essence, with the amount of dry air overhead, anticipation is that 
any meaningful rainfall will have to be convectively charged. With 
an overnight passage, conceptually, instability should be lacking, 
and thus, trends will likely be bearish with rain amounts in the 
coming days regarding Wednesday's shower potential. Through the rest 
of the week, the active rain / storm zone to our south will draw 
north a touch with time, perhaps clipping the very southern edge of 
the Great Lakes with some appreciable rain through the end of the 
week. This corridor of rain may get a charge from the remnants of 
Hurricane Polo getting ingested into the pattern... and the amount 
of moisture and forcing may be just enough to prolong low end shower 
chances Thursday through next weekend... but should be noted that 
there will be ample dry time. Wouldn't even be surprising to see the 
forecast trend dry some days given how little moisture is set to be 
drawn into our neck of the woods. Temperatures will respond to the 
shortwave passage accordingly as well... highs will trend to much 
more seasonable levels by next weekend... with highs in the low-to-
mid 60s and lows back in the 40s.
